title: Book 8 — Banquet in the house of Alcinous—the games
paragraphs: When rosy-fingered Dawn appeared at daybreak, both Alcinous and Odysseus rose, and Alcinous led the way to the Phaeacian assembly place near the ships. They sat side by side on polished stone seats while Athena took the form of one of Alcinous's servants and went through the town to help Odysseus get home. She approached each citizen individually, saying, "Leaders and councilors of the Phaeacians, come to the assembly and listen to this stranger who has just arrived at King Alcinous's house after a long voyage. He looks like an immortal god."

With these words she inspired them all to come, and they flocked to the assembly until every seat and standing space was packed. Everyone was struck by Odysseus's appearance, for Athena had enhanced his head and shoulders, making him look taller and more imposing than he really was, so that he might favorably impress the Phaeacians as a remarkable man and perform well in the many contests they would challenge him to. When they had all gathered, Alcinous spoke:

"Listen to me, leaders and councilors of the Phaeacians, so I may speak my mind. This stranger, whoever he may be, has come to my house from somewhere east or west. He needs an escort and wants the matter settled. Let us prepare one for him, as we have done for others before. Indeed, no one who has ever come to my house has been able to complain that I was slow in speeding them on their way. Let us launch a ship—one that has never made a voyage—and crew it with fifty-two of our smartest young sailors. When you have secured your oars to your benches, leave the ship and come to my house for a feast. I will provide everything. These are my instructions to the young men who will form the crew. As for you leaders and councilors, you will join me in entertaining our guest in the courtyard. I will accept no excuses, and we will have Demodocus sing for us, for there is no bard like him, whatever he chooses to sing about."

Alcinous then led the way, and the others followed, while a servant went to fetch Demodocus. The fifty-two chosen oarsmen went to the seashore as instructed, and when they arrived they launched the ship into the water, set the mast and sails inside her, bound the oars to the oarlocks with twisted leather thongs, all in proper order, and spread the white sails aloft. They moored the vessel a little way offshore, then came ashore and went to King Alcinous's house. The courtyards, grounds, and all the surrounding areas were filled with crowds of men, both old and young, in great numbers. Alcinous slaughtered twelve sheep, eight full-grown pigs, and two oxen for them. These they skinned and prepared to provide a magnificent banquet.

A servant then brought in the famous bard Demodocus, whom the Muse had dearly loved but to whom she had given both good and evil—though she had blessed him with the divine gift of song, she had taken away his eyesight. Pontonous set a chair for him among the guests, leaning it against a pillar. He hung the lyre on a peg above his head and showed him where to reach for it with his hands. He also set a fine table beside him with a basket of food and a cup of wine from which he could drink whenever he wished.

The company then began eating the good food before them, but as soon as they had finished eating and drinking, the Muse inspired Demodocus to sing about the deeds of heroes, particularly a story that was then on everyone's lips—the quarrel between Odysseus and Achilles and the harsh words they exchanged while sitting together at a banquet. Agamemnon was pleased when he heard his chieftains quarreling with each other, for Apollo had prophesied this to him at Pytho when he crossed the stone floor to consult the oracle. This was the beginning of the disaster that Zeus's will brought upon both Greeks and Trojans.

So the bard sang, but Odysseus pulled his purple cloak over his head and covered his face, ashamed to let the Phaeacians see him weeping. When the bard stopped singing, he wiped away his tears, uncovered his face, and taking his cup, made a drink offering to the gods. But when the Phaeacians urged Demodocus to continue singing, for they delighted in his songs, Odysseus again drew his cloak over his head and wept bitterly. No one noticed his distress except Alcinous, who was sitting nearby and heard the heavy sighs he was making. So he immediately said, "Leaders and councilors of the Phaeacians, we have had enough of both the feast and the music that accompanies it. Let us now proceed to athletic competitions, so that our guest can tell his friends when he returns home how much we surpass all other nations in boxing, wrestling, jumping, and running."

With these words he led the way, and the others followed. A servant hung Demodocus's lyre on its peg, led him out of the courtyard, and set him on the same path that all the Phaeacian leaders were taking to watch the sports. A crowd of several thousand people followed them, and there were many excellent competitors for all the events. There was Acroneus, Ocyalus, Elatreus, Nauteus, Prymneus, Anchialus, Eretmeus, Ponteus, Proreus, Thoon, Anabesineus, and Amphialus son of Polyneus son of Tecton. There was also Euryalus son of Naubolus, who was like Ares himself and was the handsomest man among the Phaeacians except Laodamas. Three sons of Alcinous also competed: Laodamas, Halios, and Clytoneus.

The foot races came first. They set out the course from the starting line, and they raised dust on the plain as they all sprang forward at once. Clytoneus won by a wide margin, leaving everyone else behind by the length of furrow that a pair of mules can plow in a fallow field. They then turned to the grueling art of wrestling, and here Euryalus proved to be the best man. Amphialus excelled all others in jumping, while in discus throwing no one could approach Elatreus. Alcinous's son Laodamas was the best boxer, and when they had all been entertained by the games, he said, "Let's ask the stranger if he excels in any of these sports. He seems very powerfully built—his thighs, calves, hands, and neck show tremendous strength, and he's not old at all. But he has suffered much lately, and nothing wreaks havoc on a man like the sea, no matter how strong he is."
"You're absolutely right, Laodamas," replied Euryalus. "Go up to your guest and speak to him about it yourself."

When Laodamas heard this, he made his way into the middle of the crowd and said to Odysseus, "I hope, sir, that you will enter one or another of our competitions if you're skilled in any of them—and you must have participated in many before now. Nothing brings a man such lifelong credit as showing himself capable with his hands and feet. So please try something and banish all sorrow from your mind. Your journey home won't be delayed much longer, for the ship is already launched and the crew is ready."

Odysseus answered, "Laodamas, why do you taunt me this way? My mind is focused on troubles rather than contests. I have been through endless hardship and come among you now as a suppliant, asking your king and people to help me on my journey home."

Then Euryalus insulted him outright and said, "I gather you're unskilled in any of the many sports that men usually enjoy. I suppose you're one of those greedy traders who sail around in ships as captains or merchants, thinking of nothing but their outbound cargo and return freight. You don't seem to have much of the athlete about you."

"Shame on you, sir," answered Odysseus fiercely. "You're an insolent fellow—it's true that the gods don't bless all men equally in speech, appearance, and understanding. One man may have a weak presence, but heaven has blessed him with such good conversation that he charms everyone who sees him. His smooth eloquence wins over his listeners so that he leads in all assemblies of his peers, and wherever he goes he is looked up to. Another may be as handsome as a god, but his good looks aren't matched with wisdom. This is your case. No god could make a finer-looking man than you, but you're a fool. Your ill-judged remarks have made me extremely angry, and you're quite mistaken, for I excel in many athletic events. Indeed, as long as I had youth and strength, I was among the finest athletes of my time. Now, however, I'm worn out by hardship and sorrow, for I've endured much both on the battlefield and on the weary sea. Still, despite all this, I will compete, for your taunts have stung me to the core."

So he jumped up without even removing his cloak and seized a discus—larger, more massive, and much heavier than those the Phaeacians used when throwing among themselves. Then, swinging it back, he hurled it from his powerful hand, and it hummed through the air as he did so. The Phaeacians cowered beneath the rush of its flight as it sped gracefully from his hand and flew beyond any mark that had been made yet. Athena, in the form of a man, came and marked where it had fallen. "A blind man, sir," she said, "could easily find your mark by feeling for it—it's so far ahead of any other. You can set your mind at ease about this contest, for no Phaeacian can come near such a throw as yours."

Odysseus was glad when he found he had a friend among the spectators, so he began to speak more pleasantly. "Young men," he said, "match that throw if you can, and I'll throw another discus just as heavy or even heavier. If anyone wants to have a contest with me, let him come forward, for I'm extremely angry. I'll box, wrestle, or run—I don't care which—with any of you except Laodamas, but not with him because I'm his guest, and one can't compete with one's own host. At least I don't think it's wise or sensible for a guest to challenge his host's family at any game, especially in a foreign country. He'll undermine his own position if he does. But I make no exception for anyone else, for I want to settle this matter and see who's the best man. I'm skilled at every kind of athletic sport known to mankind. I'm an excellent archer. In battle I'm always the first to bring down a man with my arrow, no matter how many others are aiming at him alongside me. Philoctetes was the only man who could shoot better than I when we Greeks were before Troy and practicing. I far surpass everyone else in the whole world among those who still eat bread on the face of the earth, but I wouldn't want to compete against the mighty dead, such as Heracles or Eurytus of Oechalia—men who could shoot against the gods themselves. This is actually how Eurytus met his premature end, for Apollo was angry with him and killed him because he challenged the god as an archer. I can throw a spear farther than anyone else can shoot an arrow. Running is the only area where I fear some of the Phaeacians might beat me, for I've been brought very low at sea. My provisions ran short, and so I'm still weak."

They all remained silent except King Alcinous, who began, "Sir, we have had much pleasure hearing all you've told us, from which I understand you're willing to show your skill, having been displeased by some insolent remarks made by one of our athletes—remarks that could never have been uttered by anyone who knows how to speak properly. I hope you'll understand my meaning and will explain to any of your chief men who may be dining with you and your family when you get home, that we have a hereditary talent for accomplishments of all kinds. We're not particularly remarkable for boxing or wrestling, but we're exceptionally fast runners and excellent sailors. We're extremely fond of good dinners, music, and dancing. We also like frequent changes of clothing, warm baths, and comfortable beds. So now, please, some of you who are the best dancers, start dancing, so that our guest can tell his friends when he returns home how much we surpass all other nations as sailors, runners, dancers, and singers. Demodocus left his lyre at my house, so someone run and fetch it for him."

At this a servant hurried off to bring the lyre from the king's house, and nine men who had been chosen as officials stepped forward. It was their job to manage everything connected with the sports, so they smoothed the ground and marked out a wide space for the dancers. Soon the servant returned with Demodocus's lyre, and he took his place in their midst. Then the best young dancers in the town began to move and dance so nimbly that Odysseus was delighted with the merry twinkling of their feet.

Meanwhile the bard began to sing about the love affair of Ares and Aphrodite, and how they first began their secret relationship in Hephaestus's house. Ares gave Aphrodite many gifts and defiled King Hephaestus's marriage bed, so the Sun, who saw what they were doing, told Hephaestus. Hephaestus was furious when he heard such dreadful news, so he went to his forge planning mischief, set up his great anvil, and began making chains that none could either loosen or break, so they would stay trapped there. When he had finished his snare, he went into his bedroom and draped the bed-posts all over with chains like spider webs. He also hung many from the great ceiling beam. Not even a god could see them, so fine and subtle were they. As soon as he had spread the chains all over the bed, he pretended to set out for the fair land of Lemnos, which of all places in the world was his favorite. But Ares kept a sharp lookout, and as soon as he saw him leave, hurried off to his house, burning with love for Aphrodite.

Now Aphrodite had just returned from visiting her father Zeus and was about to sit down when Ares came inside the house and said as he took her hand in his own, "Come to Hephaestus's bed—he's not at home, but has gone off to Lemnos among the Sintians, whose speech is foreign."

She was quite willing, so they went to the bed to rest, where they were caught in the trap that cunning Hephaestus had set for them. They could neither get up nor move hand or foot, but realized too late that they were trapped. Then Hephaestus returned to them, for he had turned back before reaching Lemnos when his spy the Sun told him what was happening. He was in a furious rage and stood in the entrance making a terrible noise as he shouted to all the gods.

"Father Zeus," he cried, "and all you other blessed gods who live forever, come here and see the ridiculous and disgraceful sight I'll show you. Zeus's daughter Aphrodite is always dishonoring me because I'm lame. She's in love with Ares, who is handsome and well-built, while I'm a cripple—but my parents are to blame for that, not I. They should never have had me. Come and see the pair together asleep on my bed. It makes me furious to look at them. They're very fond of each other, but I don't think they'll lie there longer than they have to, nor do I think they'll sleep much. There, however, they'll stay until her father has repaid me the bride-price I gave him for his worthless daughter, who is beautiful but not faithful."

At this the gods gathered at Hephaestus's house. Earth-shaking Poseidon came, and Hermes the luck-bringer, and King Apollo, but the goddesses all stayed home out of shame. Then the givers of all good things stood in the doorway, and the blessed gods roared with uncontrollable laughter as they saw how cunning Hephaestus had been. One would turn to his neighbor saying:
"Evil deeds don't prosper, and the weak confound the strong. See how limping Hephaestus, lame as he is, has caught Ares who is the swiftest god in heaven. Now Ares will have to pay heavy damages."
This is how they talked, but King Apollo said to Hermes, "Messenger Hermes, giver of good things, wouldn't you mind how strong the chains were if you could sleep with Aphrodite?"

"King Apollo," answered Hermes, "I only wish I might get the chance, even if there were three times as many chains—and all of you gods and goddesses could watch—but I would sleep with her if I could."

The immortal gods burst out laughing when they heard him, but Poseidon took it all seriously and kept urging Hephaestus to set Ares free again. "Let him go," he cried, "and I'll guarantee, as you require, that he'll pay you all the damages that are considered reasonable among the immortal gods."
"Don't," replied Hephaestus, "ask me to do this. A bad man's promise is worthless security. What remedy could I enforce against you if Ares should leave and abandon his debts along with his chains?"
"Hephaestus," said Poseidon, "if Ares goes away without paying his damages, I'll pay you myself." So Hephaestus answered, "In that case I cannot and must not refuse you."

Then he loosened the bonds that held them, and as soon as they were free they rushed off—Ares to Thrace and laughter-loving Aphrodite to Cyprus and to Paphos, where her grove and altar fragrant with offerings are located. There the Graces bathed her and anointed her with ambrosial oil such as the immortal gods use, and they clothed her in the most enchanting garments.
So the bard sang, and both Odysseus and the seafaring Phaeacians were charmed as they listened to him.

Then Alcinous told Laodamas and Halius to dance alone, since there was no one to compete with them. So they took a red ball that Polybus had made for them, and one bent backward and threw it up toward the clouds while the other jumped from the ground and caught it easily before it came down again. When they had finished throwing the ball straight up into the air, they began to dance while simultaneously tossing it back and forth to each other, as all the young men in the circle applauded and stamped their feet loudly. Then Odysseus said:
"King Alcinous, you said your people were the nimblest dancers in the world, and indeed they have proved themselves to be so. I was amazed as I watched them."

The king was delighted at this and exclaimed to the Phaeacians, "Leaders and town councilors, our guest seems to be a person of exceptional judgment. Let us give him such proof of our hospitality as he may reasonably expect. There are twelve chief men among you, and counting myself there are thirteen. Each of you contribute a clean cloak, a shirt, and a talent of fine gold. Let us give him all this together at once, so when he has his dinner he may do so with a light heart. As for Euryalus, he will have to make a formal apology and give a present too, for he has been rude."

So he spoke, and the others all applauded his words and sent their servants to fetch the presents. Then Euryalus said, "King Alcinous, I will give the stranger all the satisfaction you require. He shall have my sword, which is bronze except for the hilt, which is silver. I'll also give him the scabbard of newly carved ivory that it fits into. It will be worth a great deal to him."

As he spoke he placed the sword in Odysseus's hands and said, "Good luck to you, respected stranger. If anything has been said inappropriately, may the winds blow it away, and may heaven grant you a safe return, for I understand you've been long away from home and have endured much hardship."
To which Odysseus answered, "Good luck to you too, my friend, and may the gods grant you every happiness. I hope you won't miss the sword you've given me along with your apology."

With these words he strapped the sword to his shoulders, and toward sunset the presents began to arrive as the servants of the donors kept bringing them to King Alcinous's house. His sons received them and placed them in their mother's care. Then Alcinous led the way to the house and had his guests take their seats.

"Wife," he said, turning to Queen Arete, "go fetch the finest chest we have and put a clean cloak and shirt in it. Also, put a pot on the fire and heat some water. Our guest will take a warm bath. See also to the careful packing of the presents that the noble Phaeacians have given him. This way he'll better enjoy both his dinner and the singing that will follow. I'll personally give him this golden goblet—which is exquisitely crafted—so he'll be reminded of me for the rest of his life whenever he makes a drink offering to Zeus or any of the gods."

Then Arete told her maids to put a large tripod on the fire as quickly as they could, so they set a tripod full of bath water over a clear fire. They threw on sticks to make it blaze, and the water became hot as the flame played around the belly of the tripod. Meanwhile Arete brought a magnificent chest from her own room, and inside it she packed all the beautiful presents of gold and clothing that the Phaeacians had brought. Finally she added a cloak and a fine shirt from Alcinous and said to Odysseus:
"See to the lid yourself and have the whole thing tied up at once, in case anyone should rob you while you're sleeping in your ship."

When Odysseus heard this, he put the lid on the chest and secured it with a knot that Circe had taught him. He had barely finished when a servant told him to come to the bath and wash himself. He was very glad of a warm bath, for he had had no one to wait on him ever since he left Calypso's house, who had taken as good care of him as if he were a god as long as he stayed with her. When the servants had finished washing and anointing him with oil and had given him a clean cloak and shirt, he left the bathroom and joined the guests who were sitting over their wine. Lovely Nausicaa stood by one of the pillars supporting the roof of the courtyard and admired him as she saw him pass. "Farewell, stranger," she said. "Don't forget me when you're safe at home again, for it's to me first that you owe thanks for saving your life."

And Odysseus said, "Nausicaa, daughter of great Alcinous, may Zeus the mighty husband of Hera grant that I reach my home. Then I shall bless you as my guardian angel all my days, for it was you who saved me."

When he had said this, he seated himself beside Alcinous. Dinner was then served, and wine was mixed for drinking. A servant led in the celebrated bard Demodocus and seated him in the middle of the company, near one of the pillars supporting the courtyard, so he could lean against it. Then Odysseus cut off a piece of roast pork with plenty of fat (for there was abundance left on the joint) and said to a servant, "Take this piece of pork to Demodocus and tell him to eat it. Despite any pain his songs may cause me, I will honor him nonetheless. Bards are honored and respected throughout the world, for the Muse teaches them their songs and loves them."

The servant carried the pork over to Demodocus, who took it and was very pleased. They then began eating the good food before them, and as soon as they had finished eating and drinking, Odysseus said to Demodocus, "Demodocus, there is no one in the world I admire more than you. You must have studied under the Muse, Zeus's daughter, and under Apollo, so accurately do you sing about the Greeks' return with all their sufferings and adventures. If you weren't there yourself, you must have heard it all from someone who was. Now, however, change your song and tell us about the wooden horse that Epeus made with Athena's help, which Odysseus got by trickery into Troy's fortress after filling it with the men who later sacked the city. If you sing this tale properly, I'll tell all the world how magnificently heaven has blessed you."

The heaven-inspired bard took up the story at the point where some of the Greeks set fire to their tents and sailed away while others, hidden within the horse, were waiting with Odysseus in Troy's assembly place. For the Trojans themselves had dragged the horse into their fortress, and it stood there while they sat in council around it, unable to decide what to do. Some wanted to break it up then and there; others would have it dragged to the top of the rock where the fortress stood and then thrown down the cliff; while still others wanted to let it remain as an offering to appease the gods. And this is how they decided in the end, for the city was doomed when it accepted that horse, within which were all the bravest Greeks waiting to bring death and destruction to the Trojans. Then he sang how the Greeks emerged from the horse and sacked the town, breaking out from their hiding place. He sang how they overran the city in all directions and ravaged it, and how Odysseus went raging like Ares along with Menelaus to Deiphobus's house. It was there that the fighting was fiercest, but nevertheless with Athena's help he was victorious.

All this he told, but Odysseus was overcome as he heard him, and his cheeks were wet with tears. He wept as a woman weeps when she throws herself on the body of her husband who has fallen before his own city and people, fighting bravely to defend his home and children. She screams aloud and throws her arms around him as he lies gasping for breath and dying, but her enemies beat her from behind on the back and shoulders and carry her off into slavery, to a life of labor and sorrow, and the beauty fades from her cheeks. Just as pitifully did Odysseus weep, but none of those present noticed his tears except Alcinous, who was sitting near him and could hear the sobs and sighs he was making. The king therefore immediately rose and said:

"Leaders and town councilors of the Phaeacians, let Demodocus stop his song, for there are those present who don't seem to enjoy it. From the moment we finished dinner and Demodocus began to sing, our guest has been groaning and lamenting the whole time. He's evidently in great distress, so let the bard stop, that we may all enjoy ourselves, hosts and guest alike. This will be much more appropriate, for all these festivities—the escort and the presents we're giving so willingly—are entirely in his honor, and anyone with even a modest sense of propriety knows he should treat a guest and suppliant as if he were his own brother.

"Therefore, sir, don't maintain any more secrecy or reserve about what I'm going to ask you. It would be more courteous of you to give me a straight answer. Tell me the name your father and mother used to call you, and by which you were known among your neighbors and fellow citizens. No one, neither rich nor poor, is completely without a name, for people's parents give them names as soon as they're born. Tell me also your country, nation, and city, so our ships may set their course accordingly and take you there. For the Phaeacians have no pilots; their vessels have no rudders like those of other nations, but the ships themselves understand what we're thinking and want. They know all the cities and countries in the whole world and can cross the sea just as well even when it's covered with mist and cloud, so there's no danger of being wrecked or coming to harm. Still, I do remember hearing my father say that Poseidon was angry with us for being too generous in giving people escorts. He said that one day he would wreck one of our ships as it was returning from escorting someone and bury our city under a high mountain. This is what my father used to say, but whether the god will carry out his threat is a matter he will decide for himself.

"And now, tell me truthfully: Where have you been wandering, and what countries have you traveled through? Tell us about the peoples themselves and their cities—who were hostile, savage, and uncivilized, and who, on the other hand, were hospitable and humane. Tell us also why you're made so unhappy by hearing about the return of the Greek warriors from Troy. The gods arranged all this and sent them their misfortunes so that future generations might have something to sing about. Did you lose some brave relative of your wife's when you were at Troy? A son-in-law or father-in-law—who are a man's nearest relations outside his own flesh and blood? Or was it some brave and kind-hearted comrade—for a good friend is as dear to a man as his own brother?"
